turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Howzit, come through and sit. What's brought you in?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ag, I'm fine, honestly. My wife made the booking. I got stuck at the robot on Main Road forever because of load shedding, so I'm a bit rattled, but me, I'm alright.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Shame. What is she actually worried about?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): She says I don't sleep, I just lie there staring, and in the day I'm like a ghost on the couch. I told her it's nothing, but she wouldn't drop it.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright, let's start with the nights. What happens once you're in bed?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): I drop off okay, hey, around ten. Then I'm awake at three, sometimes half past two, and that's me finished. I just listen to the dogs and the fridge humming.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): And by morning, do you feel as if you've slept?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I'm wrecked. Coffee doesn't touch it. I used to do the early shift no problem, now the kettle feels like a project.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long has this waking been going on?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Eish. Months. I can't put a date on it. Last winter, or the one before. I mix those years up, sorry.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Was something going on around then, at home or at work?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Both, maybe. My dad went, and I lost the job at the depot. Which one came first I couldn't tell you. The dates are just mush in my head.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm sorry about your dad. Tell me about the job.

[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Depot supervisor, logistics, the big warehouse by the highway. Twenty two years. A new manager arrived, all spreadsheets, and they said the post was redundant. Redundant, after twenty two years.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's a heavy blow. How's your energy through the day?

[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Flat. I manage the school run if I push, then I'm on the couch till my wife gets home. She's a nurse, did I mention, so some weeks she's on nights and the house is dead quiet.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): And your mood itself? Have you been feeling down, or low in yourself?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I'm fine. Mood's alright. I'm not depressed, if that's where this is going. I'm just tired.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): What about the things you usually enjoy? Rugby, a braai, seeing people?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Rugby's still rugby, I put it on. The rest is fine. I'm not avoiding anybody.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Speaking of braais, the neighbour had a massive one, boerewors and chops, and their new dog stole a sausage clean off the plate. I didn't hang about, though. Funny dog.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): You didn't hang about. Is that just the once, or have you been pulling back from people?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah. Ja. I suppose I have. I don't pitch anymore. Can't be bothered to talk. Even the rugby, it's on and I'm not watching. I wasn't straight with you just now.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): I appreciate you correcting that. Is there sadness with it, or a heaviness?

[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): There is. I feel heavy. Some mornings I sit in the bakkie after drop-off and I just cry, which is mad, I'm forty six and I'm crying at a robot. I didn't want to come in and say I'm depressed, but it's been like that.

[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thank you. I need to ask this gently, and it's something I ask everyone, not because I assume the worst. Have you had thoughts of hurting yourself, or of not wanting to be here?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Definitely not. I've never thought that. I've got the two boys, it's not in my head at all.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm glad that's clear. How's your appetite been?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Eating's normal. She cooks, I finish the plate. I haven't lost any weight.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any headaches, or feeling sick in your stomach, along with this?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): No headaches. My stomach's fine. The coffee at your front desk is another story, mind, I wouldn't give that to an enemy.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Concentration, paperwork, driving?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Driving's okay once I'm moving. Forms, though, I lose the plot. The unemployment papers, I stare and nothing goes in. That's new for me.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Are you drinking more in the evenings to get through?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Two beers, most nights, once the kids are down. Not brandy like my uncle used to. I don't smoke, never have. The beers don't even make me sleepy.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Who's in the house with you?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): My wife Naledi, and the boys, eight and eleven. We rent in Glenwood. She's been carrying the money since the job went, and that makes me feel useless, but ja.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have you tried any tablets for the sleep or the mood?

[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja. The GP at the day hospital put me on citalopram, twenty milligrams, one in the morning. I stopped it in March. My jaw went tight and I felt like I was buzzing, so I left it.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stopped in March. Was there anything else on that script?
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Zopiclone, seven point five milligrams. I only took it once. I was a zombie the whole next day, so I binned the box.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): They also wrote amitriptyline, a small dose, supposed to help sleep. I never fetched it from the chemist. Never took one. It's not even in the house.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): So the citalopram you stopped, the zopiclone you took once, the amitriptyline you never started. Any allergies to medicines, or foods, or anything else?
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing. No penicillin thing, no foods. My sister comes out in a rash with bees, but that's her, not me.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any operations, diabetes, blood pressure, thyroid problems?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): No operations. No sugar, no pressure. I'm boring on paper. My dad had a heart attack, that's what took him, I don't know if you need that.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll note it, yes, your dad's heart attack sits in the family history. For you I'm not hearing a chronic list.

[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me take your pressure while we sit. One thirty two over eighty four, and your pulse is seventy six, regular. You look tidy enough, but your face has been flat, and you welled up talking about the bakkie.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, sorry. The school wants money for a tour and I nearly said yes before I remembered I'm not earning. Eish, that one hit me in the parking lot.

[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): The money worry is sitting right in the middle of this, I think. Let me think out loud so it's not a black box. Early waking, no energy, you've lost interest, you're tearful, and it sits somewhere in the last winter or two, after the job and your dad. My working impression is a depressive episode, not a label I'm carving in stone today.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Grief might be tangled through it. I can't cleanly say it's only the redundancy or only your dad, so I'm keeping both possibilities open.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): So I'm not losing my mind. I thought you'd tell me to have a braai and get over it.
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): No. And I'm not starting a tablet today. You already stopped the citalopram, and I don't want to hand you another one before we've watched the next couple of weeks.
[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): If you're still this low when I see you again, we might start sertraline at a small dose, but only if you want it and only if nothing has lifted. Not today.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): I'd rather skip tablets if I can. That buzzing scared me off. If you say we look again in two weeks, I can live with that.

[SEG0056] person_1 (DOCTOR): On the tiredness, I'm not sending bloods today either. If it hasn't eased by that visit, we might check your thyroid and a full blood count, so a physical cause isn't hiding in there.

[SEG0057] person_1 (DOCTOR): What I do want you to try, starting tonight, is dull and it works more often than people think. Same time out of bed every morning, twenty minutes outside in the light, and shift those beers earlier or skip them.
[SEG0058] person_1 (DOCTOR): And if any thought of hurting yourself shows up, even a small one, you don't wait for our appointment. Casualty, or phone the rooms, the same day. Naledi can bring you.
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): I'll do that. It's not there, I promise. She would drag me, you know her. Last week she nearly phoned you herself, then the dog ate her slipper, whole other saga.
[SEG0060] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let's see you in two weeks. Ask at reception to book it on your way out. If you slide before then, don't sit at home with it.
[SEG0061] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks, ja. Should I bring her? She talks straighter than I do when I start with I'm fine.
[SEG0062] person_1 (DOCTOR): Bring her if she's free, it helps. We'll only decide on the bloods and on sertraline then, and only if we still need to.
[SEG0063] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. Shame, thanks. I feel a bit lighter having said the crying bit out loud. Don't tell the boys about the robot, hey.
[SEG0064] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's between us. Book the two weeks at the desk, be decent to yourself this week, and I'll see you then.

clinical_uncertainties.description: The patient cannot date when the poor sleep began, saying last winter or the one before, and cannot say whether his father's death or the job loss came first.

spec.situation: Adult with poor sleep, low energy and loss of interest for months after a job loss or bereavement; partner or parent speaks for them; patient says 'I'm fine' then partly opens up; denies thoughts of self-harm clearly (doctor asks gently); medication discussed but not started today.
features: stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.
hedged_plan: the doctor hedges ('we might do a scan if it does not settle', 'let's see in two weeks'). Conditional vs planned status must follow the words.

denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.
vague_dates: the patient cannot date things ('since Diwali or after', 'last winter, or the one before'); no invented date; a date_uncertain item.

omissions.text: Patient said he falls asleep okay around 10 pm, then wakes at 2:30-3:00 am and is unable to get back to sleep.
Patient denied being depressed initially ('Mood's alright. I'm not depressed, if that's where this is going. I'm just tired') before later disclosing low mood and tearfulness.

Patient initially said he was not avoiding anybody and that rugby was still fine, then corrected himself to say he has been pulling back from people, doesn't pitch anymore, can't be bothered to talk, and even when rugby is on he is not really watching.
Driving was reported as okay once he is moving.
Amitriptyline was prescribed previously at a small dose for sleep but the patient never collected it from the pharmacy and never took any.
Citalopram was stopped in March because it caused jaw tightness and a 'buzzing' feeling.
Zopiclone caused him to feel like a zombie the whole next day after one dose, leading him to stop it.
Doctor stated he was not starting any tablet today.
Doctor said he was not sending blood tests today.
Doctor invited the patient to bring his wife to the follow-up if she is free, as it would help.

omissions.text: Patient explicitly denied being depressed at first ('Mood's alright. I'm not depressed') before later correcting himself and admitting low mood/heaviness and depression symptoms.
Normal appetite was described positively: eating is normal and he finishes meals.
No thyroid problems were denied when asked about operations, diabetes, blood pressure, thyroid problems.
Amitriptyline was prescribed previously for sleep at a small dose, but he never collected it from the chemist and never took any; it was not in the house.
Doctor stated he was not starting a tablet today specifically because the patient had already stopped citalopram and the doctor wanted to watch the next couple of weeks first.
Doctor advised same time out of bed every morning, not just a fixed morning wake-up.
Doctor said sertraline and bloods would be decided at the two-week review only if still needed.
